title: The DA Delay Tax: What a Slow Planning Approval Really Costs a Property Developer
linkedin:
World Town Planning Day was this week. Here's the finance conversation it should prompt for every property developer sitting on an active DA.

A slow council approval doesn't just move your start date.

It keeps charging you for every month you wait, usually invisibly.

Interest on land and holding finance during the approval period is almost always capitalised, added to the loan balance rather than paid in cash. No invoice lands. No cash leaves the account. The loan balance just grows a little further every month the DA sits with council.

Then there's the presale side. Most construction finance needs 60 to 70 percent of a project presold before the bank will fund the build. Those presale contracts carry sunset clauses, dates by which settlement must happen or the buyer can walk and get their deposit back.

A DA delay eats directly into the gap between when presales were locked in and when those sunset clauses expire. Buyers who signed twelve months ago at one price are settling into a market that may have moved, and some don't settle at all.

The developers who handle this well don't treat the council timeline as a risk to hope away. They model three scenarios, on schedule, three months over, six months over, and know exactly where the margin breaks in each one, before the bank asks.

Full piece on the ProfitPulse blog.

Ever wondered why a "fully approved and ready to build" development can still blow its budget before a single brick goes down?

It's usually the wait, not the build. Interest on land finance keeps compounding quietly while council assesses the application, and buyers who signed off-the-plan contracts a year ago have a deadline of their own ticking over at the same time.

None of it shows up as a line item until settlement, when it's suddenly very real.

If you're a developer, how closely does your feasibility study actually account for the council clock, not just the construction one?

A note this week for property developers across Brisbane, Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria, timed to World Town Planning Day.

The pattern we see often with development projects is that the real financial risk isn't the build, it's the wait beforehand. While a development application sits with council, land and holding finance interest usually keeps accruing in the background, added to the loan balance rather than paid in cash. Nothing shows up as an obvious cost until settlement, when it's repaid out of sale proceeds alongside everything else.

At the same time, most construction finance depends on a presale threshold being met, and those presale contracts carry sunset dates. A longer than expected council timeline can push up against those dates right when the funding is meant to come together.

The developers who manage this best build more than one planning timeline into their feasibility study from the start, rather than relying on the best case date alone.
